explanation: Process concentric square layers. Emit the top, right, bottom and left sides with one endpoint excluded on each side, so corners appear once. A one-cell innermost layer is emitted separately.
timeComplexity: O(n³) for this code: each of Θ(n) layers constructs list(zip(*square_matrix)) twice, costing Θ(n²) per layer; emitting cells costs O(n²). Account for each layer’s actual loops and, in Python, its full matrix transpositions.
spaceComplexity: O(n²) transient transposed matrix storage, in addition to O(n²) output. Boundary indices are constant-sized; the output holds every matrix entry. Python additionally builds full transposed matrices.
attribution: Unmodified reference from epi_judge_python_solutions/spiral_ordering.py; Elements of Programming Interviews Judge contributors; CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 International, retained in repository LICENSE. Explanation authored for EPI Practice.
correctness: The side ranges partition a layer into four disjoint clockwise segments. Removing that layer leaves the next smaller square; induction covers every cell once. The center case handles the only layer whose four sides would otherwise overlap.
walkthrough: For [[21, 22, 23], [31, 32, 33], [41, 42, 43]], read the top row 21, 22, 23; the right edge 33, 43; the bottom edge backward 42, 41; and the left edge upward 31. Only center 32 remains. Return [21, 22, 23, 33, 43, 42, 41, 31, 32]. The walkthroughCase uses the judge’s JSON input format and expected observation.
edgeCases: An empty square produces no output.
A 1 by 1 square emits its center once.
Odd-sized matrices have a final center; even-sized matrices finish with a ring and no repeated cells.
